title: FlashCart — the bus and the gate

panels.title: Oldest unpublished message (seconds)
panels.description: The number that actually matters. Depth alone cannot tell a busy relay from a dead one — under a flash sale a deep queue is correct. An old row never is.

panels.title: Outbox depth
panels.description: Queued messages awaiting the relay. A steady small number is normal under load; a line that only climbs is a relay that has stopped.

panels.title: Relay throughput vs send failures
panels.description: A single poisoned row retried every tick climbs the failure line while depth stays at one — a different shape from a broker outage.

panels.title: The availability gate — is it earning its place?
Gate decisions
panels.description: REFUSED is the gate's entire reason to exist: requests answered without touching a connection. If it stays near zero under load, the gate is pure overhead. A sustained UNKNOWN rate means Redis is unreachable and the gate is doing nothing — while the platform stays perfectly correct, because PostgreSQL still decides.

panels.title: Share of requests refused before the database
panels.description: The gate's payoff, as a fraction. Everything else still reached PostgreSQL, where the conditional UPDATE decided it.

panels.title: The saga — where orders are going
Order transitions
panels.description: Tagged from → to, so the compensation paths are legible without reading the code. PAYMENT_PENDING → PAYMENT_FAILED and RESERVED → RESERVATION_EXPIRED are the two that say the platform is losing orders, and to what.

panels.title: Transitions the state machine declined
panels.description: Should sit at zero. Since Phase 8, duplicates are caught by processed_events before reaching the guard, so anything here is a transition that was genuinely attempted and should not have been.

panels.title: Operator access — who is reading whose data
Operator reads of another customer's data
panels.description: Every operator read of somebody else's payment, parcel or order, by action. A customer reading their own is not counted and never will be — that is the ordinary path, and including it would bury the handful of events worth reviewing under all the traffic nobody needs to look at. There is no threshold on this: how much operator reading is normal is a business fact, not a fault. It is here so that a change in the pattern is visible to somebody who looks.

panels.title: Operator reads refused because the access could not be recorded
panels.description: Should sit at zero. When it does not, operator_access_log is unwritable and the service is refusing operator reads rather than serving one unrecorded (ADR 0025). Customers reading their own data are unaffected. This is the panel that alerts, because unlike the one beside it this is wrong on its own terms.

panels.title: Refunds completed
panels.description: Captures reversed because a customer cancelled a paid order before it was dispatched (ADR 0030). No threshold: how many people change their minds is a business fact, and an alert on it would be a guess dressed as a fault. A rise here is a question for whoever runs the sale, not for whoever is on call.

panels.title: Refunds the provider refused — money still held
panels.description: Should sit at zero. Anything else is a capture the provider would not reverse for an order that is already CANCELLED: the customer has been told they are getting their money back and they are not. This is the panel that alerts. Nothing retries these yet (ADR 0030), so find them with: select * from payments where status = 'REFUND_FAILED'.

panels.title: Refunds given up on — money owed, nothing trying
panels.description: The escalation of the panel beside it. The retry job (ADR 0031) hit its attempt cap, so nothing will attempt this refund again on its own. The payment is still REFUND_FAILED and still refundable — giving up on retrying is not deciding the money is not owed. Pages, unlike the refusal count, because no further automatic step exists.

panels.title: Cancellation requests re-asked
panels.description: Orders waiting in CANCELLATION_REQUESTED whose answer never arrived, where the backstop has put the question to shipping again (ADR 0031). A spike is a lost message and is what the backstop is for. A line that does not return to zero means shipping is not answering at all, and the customers behind those orders are being told neither that they were refunded nor that they were not.
